Judicial Branch testimony neither for nor against LD 1706, An Act Regarding
Notification of Appointment of Legal Representation for Indigent Clients in
Custody:
Senator Camey, Representative Kuhn, members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Judiciary, my name is Julie Finn and I represent the Judicial Branch. I would like to provide some brief testimony neither for nor against LD 1706.
This bill requires docketing of the assignment of defense counsel within 24 hours of appointment, if the defendant is incarcerated. The current process of assigmnent, docketing, and communication of assigmnents has evolved recently to include real-time updates and frequent
interactions with the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services (MCPDS), in order to
expedite the assignment of counsel.

Court clerks are directed to place a priority on fulfilling attorney requests for appointment, docketing the orders of appointment and sending notification to the attorney and to
MCPDS by email.' This is a high`-level duty assigned to the clerks who will continue to look for`
an attorney for up to 72 hours unless there is no attorney on the roster. Once the clerk determines
that there is no attorney available, they will provide to MCPDS the names of the cases that need
counsel through a SharePoint site set up for this purpose. This system has been created very recently to allow for frequent, up-to--the-minute sharing and updating of information between the
Judicial Branch and MCPDS.
Email notification uses the email address from the MCPDS attorney roster. The email
includes all of the important information that the assigned attorney needs such as future court
dates and information regarding the specifics of the case. A copy of the appointment order is also
sent to MCPDS.
When the clerk dockets the assignment into either MEJIS or Enterprise Justice, this action also generates a daily electronic notification to MCPDS.

Wliile the clerks are already instructed to prioritize the notification of attorneys after
appointment to a criminal case, they are responsible for many other high-priority, time sensitive tasks as well. The clerks are instructed, for example, to release bail (immediately or same day),

JAF testimony 4/25/25

post bail conditions (same day when bond is executed by the court or within 72 hours for bail
issued by the jail or bail commissioner), post protection orders to the Metro switch (immediately or same day), docket and send email notification for Change of Custody Orders in child protection cases (within 24 hours), process juvenile sealing orders (within 5 business days),
process all mail as new pleadings come in (daily), issue paperwork for the jail (daily), and
process financials (daily).
LD 1706 essentially seeks to prioritize the clerks' Workload, which is not an area that
requires legislative intervention. As stated above, (1) the clerks are already instructed to communicate attorney assigmnents urgently, and (2) there are other competing priorities that are
also time sensitive.
During the budget process, the Judicial Branch indicated to this committee that more clerk positions are necessary in order to appropriately staff our comts. To the extent that the appointments are not emailed Within 24 hours currently, it is due to staffing issues. Thus, if this
bill were to receive a positive vote in committee, it would be necessary to assess how many clerk
positions would be necessary to meet the requirements of LD 1706.
Thank you for your time. I would be happy to answer any questions.

April 24, 2025
Senator Anne Carney, Chair Representative Amy Kuhn, Chair Esteemed members of the Joint Committee on Judiciary 5 State House Station, Room 438 Augusta, ME 04333
RE: LD 1706: An Act Regarding Notification of Appointment of Legal Representation for Indigent Clients in Custody
Dear Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the esteemed Judiciary Committee:
My name is Trey Cox, I'm a recent graduate of Maine Law who caught a passion for public defense during my time at the Cumberland Legal Aid Clinic and have had the pleasure of working as a public defender on the Public Defense Services roster since joining the Maine State Bar.
I write in support of this bill, which addresses a vital delay in the appointment system that often effects the most vulnerable defendants.
There will always be delay between when an incarcerated individual is given the name of their attorney and when the attorney receives the appointment. Each time I have joined the roster to receive new cases, I get contacted by incarcerated clients immediately after I am appointed to their case in court. When this happens, I take them at their word and start working on their cases while I await docketing and incoming appointment documents.
Unfortunately, not all clients reach out. Many incarcerated individuals have language barriers, mental health difficulties, illnesses, or other conditions that prevent them from reaching out to their attorneys with the information provided by the Court. These defendants, many of whom may be released to the community under updated bail conditions, would be protected by the practice put forward by this bill.
I have experienced multiple cases where the delay between appointment and notification (via docketing) has been over two weeks. While courts today are backlogged, docketing attorney appointments for incarcerated individuals should be a priority for the Court as without it, attorneys have no way of knowing that they have a client in-custody. For many, delay of a few days can be the difference that causes them to lose housing, employment, or other important pieces of living a successful, stable life.
I encourage you all to vote "ought to pass" on this important bill to assist those incarcerated individuals who need counsel most, and are deprived of our assistance due solely to administrative delays.
Sincerely,
M. Trey Cox tcox@twmmaine.com

RE: LD 1706: "An Act Regarding Notification of Appointment of Legal Representation for Indigent Clients in Custody." Dear Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn and members of the Judiciary Committee:
MACDL supports LD 1706
LD 1706 requires clerks' offices to enter orders of appointment of counsel to indigent defendants held in custody within 24 hours of the order excluding holidays and weekends.
MACDL understands this bill is meant to address situations whereby the courtappointed attorneys for incarcerated defendants may not receive notice of appointment for days or even weeks after the appointment happens in the courtroom.
Timely notice of appointment is critical to adequate defense because newly appointed counsel may seek to amend bail so that accused criminal defendants are able to return to work, home, and their families. Timely notice also means that an attorney can schedule a time to meet his or her new client in jails that often have limited hours for even attorney visits. These initial appointments are necessary to explore defenses and identify witnesses to interview.
In short, time is of the essence when people are accused of crimes and held in jail.

For all these reasons, MACDL supports LD 1706.

Thank you.

Distinguished members of the Judiciary Committee,
My Name is Norman Hightower and I'm writing this testimony in support of LD 1706, an act regarding notification of appointment of legal representatives for indigent clients in custody, on behalf of Restorative Justice Project Maine.
We believe it is imperative that individuals have access to competent representation as soon as possible when they are determined to be indigent. Many times people who cannot afford to pay an attorney are treated far differently than those who have a privately funded attorney. They are held longer in pre-trial detention because they have no one to file motions for bail hearings or other pretrial motions that could help secure their freedom through bail or possibly a dismissal. Incarcerated individuals who can't afford to hire an attorney don't have anyone working diligently to make sure their case is being heard. Thus they miss out on opportunities that could be the difference between sitting in jail waiting for their day in court or walking into court as an unshackled free person, and while everyone is presumed innocent until proven guilty, there is a distinct advantage in walking into the courtroom in your own clothes versus walking in wearing an orange jumpsuit and cuffs.
I myself have sat in county jail unable to post bail and without representation for over a month. In that time I lost all of my personal belongings, including a vehicle and housing. I lost my job also during that time. I finally ended up getting a bail reduction hearing and was able to post bail. If I had had an attorney assigned to my case sooner, that bail reduction hearing may have happened a lot sooner and I may not have had to experience such a catastrophic setback.
Having a lawyer who is invested in the interest of their client assigned early on can make a big difference in making sure everyone has the ability to properly navigate the difficult and often confusing landscape of the criminal justice system, regardless of their ability to pay.This bill is an attempt to ensure that indigent individuals are treated fairly by getting adequate counsel assigned to them in a timely manner. Restorative Justice Project Maine and I support LD 1706 and we ask that in the interest of justice, you do the same. Thank you for your time and careful consideration in this matter.
Sincerely, Norman Hightower  Restorative Services Support Specialist Restorative Justice Project Maine Email: norman@rjpmidcoast.org

Testimony of Representative Sophie Warren Presenting L.D. 1706, An Act Regarding Notification of Appointment of Legal
Representation for Indigent Clients in Custody Before the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary
Good morning, Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and respected colleagues of the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary. My name is Sophie Warren, and I represent House district 124. Thank you for the opportunity to present L.D. 1706, An Act Regarding Notification of Appointment of Legal Representation for Indigent Clients in Custody.
A defense attorney who is quite active in public defense here in Maine brought to my attention a minor technical issue in administrative delay between an order appointing counsel and the delay of that order being filed in the docket record of the case that is having serious impacts for indigent incarcerated defendants.
The intention of this bill is to ensure that any appointment of counsel for an indigent client in a criminal matter who is incarcerated at the time of the appointment is docketed by the Court within 24 hours of the Court appointment.
The only change here is ensuring the appointment is docketed in a timely manner. It will only implicate the cross over of defendants who are both deemed indigent by the court to be appointed counsel and who are presently incarcerated.
Presently, the Court will appoint counsel to an indigent defendant. In court on the day of appointment, the prosecutor on the case is in the courtroom, and either the defendant or a representative of the department of corrections will be, as well. That appointment is done in line with processes, timelines and availability that is a legitimate question of consideration by the Court and this committee, amongst many others.1 This bill is simply about what happens when that appointment is made. As it stands today, that signed Order will then be given to Court staff and later filed ("docketed") by the Court. Without clear guidance establishing the need to put this order into the record in an efficient manner, there are unintended consequences for defense counsel and clients alike.

VI, Maine Constitution Art. 1, Sec. 6; M.R.U. Crim. P. 44(a)(1); 4 M.R.S. Sec. 1804(3)(A)(2023); Rule 44 - Right to and Assignment of Counsel: https://www.courts.maine.gov/rules/text/mru_crim_p_plus_2017-5-3.pdf
District 124: Part of Scarborough

The consequences come because while that the prosecutor and client know the name of the attorney assigned, but that counsel themselves may not know for a period of as long as 2 weeks (in at least once case I saw myself) until the court has docketed the Order Appointing Counsel.
This discrepancy between the signing of the Order and the recording of that order in the docket record has led to clients calling their defense attorney and saying, "Why haven't you contacted me? It's been two weeks since you were appointed." And the attorney has no record of appointment, because the Order appointing them has not been docketed in the official court record.
This has also led to prosecutors sending sensitive discovery materials2 to an attorney who has no notice of appointment and may not have completed a conflict check to determine whether they can accept the appointment and provide fair counsel. More than anything, this is a consideration of the Sixth Amendment right to counsel,3 but there are additional dynamics here that functionally puts defense counsel and incarcerated clients on the wrong foot starting out, doesn't allow defense counsel the same information afforded to the prosecution within the same period of time, and deprives the entire system of seeing that those who can be out on bail, without further and unnecessary financial and crowding burdens on our jails.
This is a small change, but an important one.
Not only is there a question of this delay raising a legitimate question of sixth amendment right to counsel,456 the consequences are more dire for an incarcerated defendant. For an incarcerated client, this can be the difference between initiating a de novo bond hearing7 to determine and negotiate the terms of bond and getting out of jail or initiating a competency evaluation if there is an underlying mental health crisis or condition. The reason a de novo bond hearing is an automated 24-hour process is there can be obligations of work, family, childcare, or medical needs that can necessitate the recognized urgency of adjudicating the terms of being let out of jail if the court determines they pose no immediate threat to society, etc.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I am happy to answer any questions that you have.
